strengths: Carefully controlled experimental design: the LD-FPG encoder–decoder is frozen, allowing a clean, apples-to-apples comparison of three propagator families (Koopman/DMD, autoregressive MLP, score-guided Langevin) in a single latent space; this isolates the contribution of the propagation rule, which most prior work conflates with representation learning.

Broad and sensible benchmark hierarchy, from alanine dipeptide through ATLAS globular proteins (7JFL, 1R6W) to large GPCRs (A1AR, A2AR), with relevant baselines (LSS, MD-Gen, GeoTDM) and multiple complementary metrics (JSD of dihedral/coordinate distributions, contact-map correlation, TICA timescales, decorrelation times, lDDT failure time).

Honest scoping and discussion of limitations: the authors explicitly disclaim exact physical kinetics and NVE conservation, explain what a 'frame' means for the Langevin propagator, and carefully analyze why Langevin fails earlier on alanine (score quality, step-size calibration) rather than hiding the result.

Good ablation coverage (encoder width, pooling size, diffusion schedule, score query level, clipping, step size, data efficiency, frame skipping, residual vs. direct prediction, wall-clock cost) plus a reproducibility statement with code, seeds, environment file, and released latent trajectories.
The A2AR activation-surface result (TM3–6/TM3–7 free-energy valley recovery) is a compelling demonstration at a scale and functional complexity rarely attempted for learned all-atom simulators.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all three propagators (DMD, a two-layer MLP trained on one-step pairs, a latent DDPM denoiser plugged into Euler–Maruyama Langevin) are standard components; the contribution is primarily an empirical comparison/benchmark study rather than a new method, which limits impact for a top-tier AI venue.

Kinetic fidelity evidence is weaker than the claims suggest. Timescales are reported in simulation 'steps' without calibration to physical time, so 'physically interpretable timescales' is overstated; on ADP and 7JFL GLDP's TICA t1 is actually farther from ground truth than LSS, and only on 1R6W/A1AR does it win. The A2AR activation-surface analysis is largely qualitative (contour inspection) without a quantitative error metric.

The pooled 100-dim 'blind' latent is not validated as a good dynamical representation; propagators are trained on one-step transitions of this reconstruction-oriented latent, so the study cannot distinguish propagator failures from losses induced by the encoder. Freezing the encoder enables controlled comparison but caps what conclusions can be drawn about latent simulators in general.

Baseline comparison in Table 1 is incomplete and asymmetric: GeoTDM is omitted on three systems (GPU memory), MD-Gen is missing on ADP, and there are no error bars or multiple-run statistics for Table 1 (unlike Table 2), making some 'dominance' claims (e.g., A1AR) hard to assess.

Deterministic AR propagator plus tiny calibrated noise may systematically oversmooth the ensemble (the authors themselves note it 'oversmooths high-barrier regions'), so JSD wins for the NN could partly reflect a favorable bias in trajectory smoothness; the Langevin comparison also relies on hand-calibrated (T, Δt, s) per system, and the τ=0 score query is an extrapolation of the diffusion model outside its training regime.

Some inconsistency between headline framing and results: the 'Key result' message (reliable operation across scales) coexists with Langevin failing at frame 206 on alanine and Koopman/Langevin failing mid-horizon on A1AR, and the claimed trade-off is established on only two systems for the propagator comparison (ADP, A1AR), leaving generalizability of the trade-off conclusions open.

strengths: Well-motivated controlled study design: freezing the LD-FPG encoder-decoder and swapping only the propagator cleanly isolates the effect of the propagation rule, which is a methodologically sound way to answer the paper's question.

Comprehensive benchmarking hierarchy from alanine dipeptide through ATLAS proteins to GPCRs (A1AR/A2AR), with comparisons against reasonable baselines (LSS, MD-Gen, GeoTDM) including kinetic metrics (TICA timescales, decorrelation times), not just static ensemble fidelity.

Honest scoping statements: the authors explicitly disclaim NVE energy conservation, wall-clock-calibrated kinetics, and cross-protein generalization, and they openly analyze why the Langevin propagator fails early on alanine.

Substantial appendix supporting reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables for all three propagators, algorithms, data efficiency and frame-skipping ablations, wall-clock benchmarks, a released code repository with seeds and environments, and a helpful glossary for the ML audience.
The GPCR activation-surface analysis (TM3-6/TM3-7 free energy) is a functionally meaningful, biophysically grounded evaluation target that goes beyond generic distributional metrics.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all three propagators are standard, off-the-shelf components (a 2-layer MLP trained with one-step MSE, plain DMD, and a DDPM denoiser coupled to overdamped Langevin). The contribution is essentially an empirical comparison/benchmark study rather than a new method or new theory, and the encoder-propagator-decoder framing is well established (LSS, DeepGenMSM, ITO, etc.).

The headline results are mixed and partially undercut the abstract's claims: GLDP-NN loses to LSS on ADP dihedral JSD, to MD-Gen on 7JFL/1R6W contacts, and its kinetic timescales are systematically compressed relative to ground truth (7JFL: 226 vs 660; A1AR: 650 vs 1059; decorrelation 520 vs 1281). Describing these as 'coherent physical timescales' overstates the evidence.

Fairness and calibration concerns in the propagator comparison: Langevin's temperature, step size, and sampling stride are tuned per system to match reference RMSD-per-frame; Koopman's truncation rank and rollout noise are tuned per system for stability. These per-system tuning procedures can materially affect the stability and failure-time conclusions that form a core claim (Sec. 4.2).

Circularity in the stability metric: the lDDT < 0.65 'failure time' threshold is described as 'empirically calibrated' by the authors' own analysis, without an independent or pre-registered justification, yet the headline claim ('NN is most robust') rests on this threshold.

The claimed 'first learned, all-atom rollout recovering a GPCR activation surface' (Contribution 4) is under-supported: the A2AR analysis in Sec. 4.4/Fig. 4 is entirely qualitative (contour overlap and visual 1D slices), with no quantitative JSD or transition-path statistics, and the 'first' claim is not carefully substantiated against closely related latent simulators.

Key conclusions rest on a single dataset per system with limited statistical rigor: Table 1 reports no error bars or repeated runs, and several margin-of-victory comparisons (e.g., contact correlations 0.985 vs 0.980) are within plausible run-to-run noise.

The frozen LD-FPG backbone introduces a confound: reconstruction error and the pooled-latent bottleneck (d=100) could dominate downstream fidelity, but the paper provides no decomposition of propagated error into encoder, propagator, and decoder contributions.

Kinetic evaluation is conceptually fragile: propagators trained purely on one-step transitions (and score models trained on static ensembles) are then judged on long-timescale TICA behavior, and the paper itself concedes timescales are 'diagnostic rather than calibrated,' which weakens the significance of the kinetic rankings in Table 1.

strengths: Well-designed controlled study: freezing the LD-FPG encoder–decoder and swapping only the propagator cleanly isolates the effect of the propagation rule, which is a genuinely useful experimental design for the latent-space MD simulation community.
Impressive breadth of benchmark systems, spanning four orders of complexity from alanine dipeptide to GPCRs, with access to baselines (LSS, MD-Gen, GeoTDM) on the same data.

Careful and unusually honest methodological discussion: the authors explicitly disclaim NVE energy conservation and wall-clock calibrated kinetics, explain what a 'frame' means for the Langevin propagator, and give concrete failure analysis for the Langevin integrator on alanine.

Extensive supporting material: detailed hyperparameter tables, ablations on encoder width, pooled latent size, denoiser settings, data efficiency, temporal stride, residual vs. direct prediction, and wall-clock timing; a reproducibility statement with code, seeds, and preprocessed latents.

The A2AR activation-surface analysis (TM3–6/TM3–7 free-energy surfaces) is an interesting functional observable that goes beyond static ensemble metrics, and the side-chain rotamer findings (Langevin best for multi-modal rotamer bands) are a non-obvious empirical result.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all three propagators are standard, off-the-shelf techniques (plain DMD Koopman, a 2-layer MLP trained with one-step MSE, and a DDPM denoiser plus overdamped Langevin). The paper is essentially a benchmark/comparison study of known components, and the headline finding — that a deterministic autoregressive MLP is the most stable — is largely expected given the known error-accumulation behavior of one-step regression models.

The central claim that GLDP 'operates reliably across scales' is not well supported by Table 1: on ADP and 7JFL, GLDP has substantially worse kinetics than baselines (TICA t1 = 10.1 vs. 15.8 for LSS on ADP; 226 vs. 610 for LSS and 660 ground truth on 7JFL). GLDP only dominates on the largest systems, yet the abstract and summary present a stronger, more uniform story. The narrative of a 'clear three-way trade-off' is partially built on only two systems (ADP and A1AR) in Tables 2 and Figure 2.

The A2AR GPCR activation-surface result — billed as the 'first learned all-atom rollout' of a GPCR activation surface and a key contribution — is presented only qualitatively (Figure 4) with no quantitative metric (e.g., JSD over the TM3–6/TM3–7 surface, state populations, or transition-path statistics), making this headline claim difficult to assess or falsify.

The Langevin propagator requires per-system tuning of temperature, step size, sampling stride, and score clipping (Tables 8–9, in 'arbitrary units'), calibrated to match reference RMSD-per-frame. This substantial per-system tuning burden is a confound for the propagator comparison, and the early Langevin failure on alanine reads more like an implementation artifact than a fundamental property; no hyperparameter-matched tuning protocol is applied symmetrically to the other propagators.

Kinetic fidelity is incomplete even where GLDP wins: on A1AR, GLDP's decorrelation time (520) is well below ground truth (1281), and timescales are trained/diagnosed on a single reference MD trajectory with TICA fit only on ground-truth data; no error bars or multiple rollout statistics are reported for Table 1.

The pooled 100-dimensional 'blind pooling' latent discards atom-level correspondence, yet the paper claims all-atom fidelity; the interplay between latent bottleneck quality and propagator performance is analyzed only in A1AR-specific ablations and not for the other systems.

Several presentational issues: Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 contain small, hard-to-read panels; Table 1's 'Kinetics' metric mixes systems where 'closer to ground truth' is the criterion with models that diverge by large factors; and the propagation section's formalism (Eq. 1–5) is thin relative to the empirical emphasis.
